title: Relative pointed flag curve for an adjoint rank-one group
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. An $S$-group scheme is a group object in schemes over $S$, with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] over this base. A reductive $S$-group means a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] affine finite-type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] $S$-group all of whose geometric fibres are connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] and have no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup. Unipotent means that every geometric point is unipotent in a faithful matrix representation. A split maximal torus $T\hookrightarrow G$ is a closed subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] isomorphic to $\mathbf G_{m,S}^r$, $r\geq0$, maximal among tori on every geometric fibre; a torus over an algebraically closed field is a product of multiplicative groups. Here $\mathbf G_{m,S}=\operatorname{Spec}A[z,z^{-1}]$ with multiplication of units. Semisimple rank one means that the quotient of each geometric fibre by its largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup has maximal tori of dimension one; solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial. The centre is the subgroup functor of points commuting with every point after every algebra extension. Let $G$ be reductive of semisimple rank one with trivial scheme-theoretic centre and split maximal torus $T$. Zariski locally on $S$ there is a smooth closed subgroup $B\subseteq G$ containing $T$, with connected geometric fibres, such that the fppf sheaf of right cosets $G/B$ is represented by a smooth proper [def-weil-proper-morphism] $S$-scheme $X$. Here the sheaf quotient is the sheafification of $U\mapsto G(U)/B(U)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. The quotient map $p:G\to X$ has a left $G$-action induced by multiplication, and the identity of $G$ gives a section $\sigma:S\to X$, fixed by $B$. For every geometric point [def-weil-geometric-point] $\bar s:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$, $X_{\bar s}=X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1_\Omega$ and the homomorphism induced by this action identifies $G_{\bar s}$ with the automorphism group sheaf $\operatorname{Aut}_\Omega(X_{\bar s})$. The automorphism group sheaf assigns to an $\Omega$-scheme $V$ the group of $V$-automorphisms of $X_{\bar s}\times_\Omega V$. Quotient formation, the action, and the section commute with arbitrary base change. The projective line is the projective space with two homogeneous coordinates [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change].

source.place: Conrad, Proposition 4.2.7, proof through the section of the genus-zero curve, printed pp.123--124; the geometric action is the standard action of PGL2 on its Borel quotient. Relative quotient representability and properness are Theorem 2.3.6, printed pp.72--75; the cocharacter parabolic construction is Section 4.1. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this assertion in this form.

proof.text: First $G/S$ is finitely presented: its affine coordinate algebra is finite type over the Noetherian ring $A$, so apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-noetherian-finite-presentation]. By [lem-sfb-relative-reductive-centre-weight-kernel], $Z(G_{\bar s})=Z(G)_{\bar s}=1$. Apply [lem-sfb-rank-one-adjoint-projective-linear] over each algebraically closed residue field to identify $G_{\bar s}$ with $\operatorname{PGL}_2$. The torus $T_{\bar s}$ is maximal by hypothesis; [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] conjugates it to the diagonal torus. That torus is maximal since commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(z,1)$ with indeterminate $z$ forces both off-diagonal entries to vanish. Hence $r=1$ (the split-torus ranks agree by character duality [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality]). Choose a splitting $\lambda:\mathbf G_{m,S}\xrightarrow{\sim}T$, composed with $T\hookrightarrow G$.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, first paragraph, p.123; geometric classification used in the preceding paragraph. The arbitrary-centre base-change input is Theorem 3.3.4.

proof.text: Use conjugation by $\lambda$ as the action in [lem-sfb-relative-dynamic-subgroups] and set $B=P_\lambda$. It is a smooth affine finitely presented closed subgroup with geometrically connected fibres, and its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. The orbit of each $t\in T(W)$ is constant, so $T\subseteq B$ as subgroup functors. On each geometric fibre $\lambda$ is an isomorphism onto the maximal torus. Every nonzero character remains nonzero on $\lambda$, so it is regular. By [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description], $B_{\bar s}$ is a Borel subgroup, and [lem-sfb-borel-scheme-normalizer] gives $N_{G_{\bar s}}(B_{\bar s})=B_{\bar s}$ as schemes, including on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, pp.112--114; Proposition 4.2.7, proof, p.123, construction of B and its geometric normalizer.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-relative-smooth-subgroup-normalizer] to $B\subseteq G$. It gives a finitely presented closed normalizer $N$ and a closed inclusion $B\hookrightarrow N$, whose every geometric fibre is an isomorphism by step 2 and the normalizer base-change clause. The isomorphism criterion [lem-sfb-flat-geometric-fibre-open-criterion] applies: $B$ is smooth, hence flat and locally finitely presented over $S$, $N/S$ is finite type, and $B\to N$ is finitely presented. For the last assertion, write $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$, $N=\operatorname{Spec}(C/I)$, $B=\operatorname{Spec}(C/J)$; $I\subseteq J$ and the finitely generated ideal $J$ gives the finitely generated ideal $J/I$. Thus $B=N$ over the original, possibly nonreduced base. No flatness of $N$ was assumed.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, p.123: passage from geometric normalizers to B=N; Proposition 2.1.6 and the fibral criterion replace the cited general flat-family equality test.

proof.text: Fix a geometric fibre. Under the field isomorphism of step 1 and torus conjugacy, $\lambda$ becomes $t\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(t^{\pm1},1)$: character duality [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality] says an automorphism of $\mathbf G_m$ has exponent $\pm1$. The limit definition of [lem-sfb-relative-dynamic-subgroups] then gives the upper or lower triangular subgroup, since conjugation multiplies the two off-diagonal matrix entries by $t$ and $t^{-1}$. Exchange the two coordinates in the lower-triangular case. The standard column action identifies the upper triangular subgroup with the stabilizer of $[1:0]$. By [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl], projective transformations lift locally to invertible matrices and two lifts differ by a scalar. The orbit map to $\mathbf P^1$ has local lifts sending $[1:u]$ to the matrix with columns $(1,u)$ and $(0,1)$, and $[v:1]$ to the matrix with columns $(v,1)$ and $(-1,0)$, on the two affine charts [lem-weil-pbc-projective-space-standard-charts]. Two matrices have the same first-column line precisely when their ratio on the right is upper triangular. These formulas prove, as fppf sheaves on all test schemes, $G_{\bar s}/B_{\bar s}\simeq\mathbf P^1_\Omega$, with its standard left action. This fibre quotient is projective via its identity embedding.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, p.123: geometric Borel quotient is P1; explicit two-chart verification of this standard matrix calculation.

proof.text: Now apply [lem-sfb-relative-self-normalizing-quotient] to $H=B$. The smoothness, finite presentation and geometric connectedness hypotheses hold by step 2, and self-normalization holds by step 3. Step 4 gives the projectivity of every geometric quotient required for properness. We obtain a representing smooth proper $S$-scheme $X=G/B$ and its quotient map $p:G\to X$, with $X_{\bar s}\simeq\mathbf P^1_\Omega$. This uses no relative identification of $G$ with a matrix group and no trivialization of the family $X$.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.6(1),(2), pp.72--75, applied in Proposition 4.2.7, proof, pp.123--124, before trivializing the curve.

proof.text: Left multiplication descends to the quotient by the formula $a(g,hB)=(gh)B$: replacing $h$ by $hb$ does not change its right coset. The formulas $a(1,x)=x$ and $a(g,a(h,x))=a(gh,x)$ follow from the same identities in $G$ and hold on the quotient sheaf, hence on its representing scheme. Put $\sigma=p\circ e$, with $e$ the identity section of $G$; for $b\in B$ one has $bB=B$, so $B$ fixes $\sigma$. The base-change assertion for the represented quotient in [lem-sfb-relative-self-normalizing-quotient], together with the base-change assertion for $B$ in step 2, identifies the pullback quotient with $G_{S\prime}/B_{S\prime}$. Under this identification multiplication and identity are literally the pulled-back group maps, so the displayed action and section pull back to the same formulas. This proves every asserted base-change compatibility, for arbitrary $S\prime\to S$.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, pp.123--124, quotient base change, identity section and left translation action.

proof.text: Finally, in the geometric-fibre quotient coordinates constructed in step 4 the homomorphism from $G_{\bar s}$ to automorphisms of $X_{\bar s}$ is the standard projective matrix action. Apply [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl] with $r=2$ over $\Omega$: it identifies the entire automorphism sheaf of $\mathbf P^1_\Omega$ on $\Omega$-schemes with $\operatorname{PGL}_{2,\Omega}$ by that action. Thus this homomorphism is an isomorphism of group sheaves, rather than merely a bijection of geometric points. All constructions above are available on $S$ after choosing the given torus splitting, and in particular give the required Zariski-local conclusion.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.7, proof, p.124, geometric-fibre assertion about the action on G/B; projective automorphisms as in Exercise 1.6.3(iv).
